newsitem.title: FINLAND: Outokumpu upbeat on Asia, Russia prospects.
newsitem.headline: Outokumpu upbeat on Asia, Russia prospects.

text.p: Finnish mining and metals group Outokumpu Oy sees strong growth in demand for metals and metal products in the emerging markets of Asia and Russia, the company said in a bi-annual news bulletin received on Tuesday.

Outokumpu pointed to soaring consumption of metals in Asia during the past decade and to infrastructure modernisation plans, typified by China's Three Gorges hydropower dam, requiring further "huge expenditures".
"Even assuming, conservatively, that (only) 50 percent of the projects are realised it means that consumption of metals will continue to grow strongly," Outokumpu said.

It saw potential for "massive increases" in copper consumption in China, where current per capita consumption of about 0.8 kg per year trails levels of about 10-13 kg in leading industrialised countries.
"Even small increases in per capita consumption (of copper in China) would translate into massive increases in refined offtake," it said.
"A 0.2 kg per person increase in per capita consumption would lift copper demand by 240,000 tonnes per year, equivalent to Canada's or Australia's entire annual copper consumption," Outokumpu said.
In addition to demand potential, the company painted a favourable picture of the business environment in Asia.
"Southeast Asia is perhaps the most flexible labour market in the world," it said.

Outokumpu also referred to growth potential for metals producers through the rapid development of the power industry and auto manufacturing in Asia, as well as in air-conditioning equipment, for which it already produces tubing in China.
"New markets and new technologies are clearly features of our future," CEO Jyrki Juusela said in the bulletin.
The company obtained its first manufacturing presence in Asia in November with the inauguration of a copper tubing plant at Zhongshan in China's southern province of Guangdong, Juusela added.
On Monday, Outokumpu announced it would build a copper products plant in Malaysia.
Looking at prospects in the former Soviet Union, Outokumpu saw operating conditions for international firms becoming more favourable in the long run.

"Outokumpu has a special opportunity to play an active role in the transition process in the CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) countries and gain special benefit from the emerging markets," it said.
"Metals and minerals may well be part of the engine that drives the Russian and other CIS economies to growth."
Demand for cooper products in the former Soviet Union could be expected to grow from present modest levels with growth in construction activities.
"Outokumpu's involvement in the CIS markets can reflect all aspects of its operations," it added.
So far, Outokumpu's activities in Russia had led to partnerships or full ownership of six local companies, while capital investments had been modest because of the nature of the operations, it said.
"But the six companies pave the way for potential larger-scale investments in possible future mining projects, base metals production or metal products manufacture in the region."
The company's metal purchases from the former Soviet Union could also support Outokumpu technology sales, as Outokumpu can accept metals and scrap as payment for technology.

Outokumpu said it saw further room for cooperation with Russia's Norilsk Nickel after agreeing in October 1996 on enhanced cooperation in metals trade, technology exchange, joint mining and metals production, and financing.

Norilsk's research and development activities and machinery equipment manufacturing as well as its extensive ore reserves gave the company opportunities to move downstream in its production, as Outokumpu had done.
"As a result, joining forces would be quite natural for Outokumpu and Norilsk Nickel," it said.
Outokumpu had extended its Nordic exploration activities across the Finnish-Russian border into an area four times larger than Finland, it said.

The company's approach to Russian exploration was to enter into low-risk projects at the earliest possible phase, Outokumpu said, adding that it would take at least 10 years to get from prospecting to mine operation.
"Outokumpu considers this interim the right time frame for conditions in Russia to become more favourable for international mining companies."
--John Acher, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 235
